common_name: Balearic St. John's Wort (Warty St. John's Wort)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring once frost danger has passed, into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun.

directions: This compact, aromatic evergreen subshrub is endemic to the rocky hillsides and cliffs of Mallorca, Menorca, and Ibiza, where it grows wedged into limestone crevices in full exposure. Its most distinctive feature is the texture of its leaves and stems, which are covered in small raised warty glands that release a resinous, balsamic scent when brushed or crushed. In summer it produces bright golden-yellow, five-petaled flowers with prominent stamens held just above the foliage. It requires gritty, fast-draining soil and resents winter wet, making it a favorite of Mediterranean-climate rock gardens and gravel plantings in regions with mild, dry winters.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant small nursery specimens in spring into lean, alkaline, well-drained soil, since this shrub establishes slowly and dislikes disturbance once rooted.

directions: Spurge olive is a slow-growing, olive-leaved evergreen shrub native to rocky maquis and garrigue across the western Mediterranean, including the Balearic Islands, and valued by specialist Mediterranean-plant nurseries for its tidy, drought-proof habit. Small three-petaled yellow flowers appear in late spring, followed by its namesake fruit: clusters of three fused, pea-sized berries that ripen from green to black, giving the species its epithet tricoccon ('three-seeded'). The narrow, leathery, gray-green leaves and dense twiggy framework give it an olive-like appearance even though it is unrelated to true olives. It thrives in lean, alkaline, sharply drained soil in full sun and is best propagated from semi-ripe cuttings, as seed germination is notoriously slow.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Sow scarified seed or set out young plants in spring into gritty, lean soil, as this taprooted cushion plant resents transplanting once mature.

directions: This low, silvery-haired cushion subshrub is endemic to limestone rock faces and screes of the Balearic Islands, where it forms dense mats of small pinnate, felted leaves. In spring it bears short clusters of pink to purplish pea-shaped flowers held just above the foliage. It is grown by alpine and rock-garden specialists for its compact, drought-tolerant habit and silvery foliage texture rather than for floral abundance, and it demands scree-like drainage with minimal summer water to avoid crown rot. Being deep-rooted once established, it is best started from seed or purchased as a young plant and sited permanently rather than moved.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online
